title: Greenland shark: the vertebrate that may outlive Saint Petersburg
description:
The Greenland shark is the longest-living vertebrate known to science: a large female was estimated at about 392 ± 120 years using radiocarbon in her eye lens. Here's how scientists measured it.
#greenlandshark #shorts #nature #ocean

scenes.narration: This shark might be older than Saint Petersburg. Seriously.
scenes.imagePrompt: huge slow greenland shark gliding through dark icy arctic water, faint light beams, floating particles, deep midnight blue palette with cyan highlights, cinematic lighting, shallow depth of field, no text

scenes.narration: Meet the Greenland shark. It cruises slowly through the icy waters of the Arctic and the North Atlantic.
scenes.imagePrompt: underside of arctic sea ice seen from below, cold blue light, deep midnight blue palette with cyan highlights, cinematic lighting, shallow depth of field, no text

scenes.narration: It grows painfully slowly, less than a centimeter a year. Yet it can reach over five meters long.
scenes.imagePrompt: long shark silhouette next to a glowing measuring scale in dark water, deep midnight blue palette with cyan highlights, cinematic lighting, shallow depth of field, no text

scenes.narration: Its age was read from the lens of its eye. The core forms before birth and barely changes after that.
scenes.imagePrompt: extreme close-up of a shark eye in dark water, reflective lens, deep midnight blue palette with cyan highlights, cinematic lighting, shallow depth of field, no text

scenes.narration: Scientists measured the radiocarbon inside it. And the time stamp? Traces left by nuclear tests in the fifties.
scenes.imagePrompt: laboratory with sample vials and a mass spectrometer, cool blue light, deep midnight blue palette with cyan highlights, cinematic lighting, shallow depth of field, no text

scenes.narration: The largest female came out at around three hundred ninety-two years old. Even with the margin of error, most likely at least two hundred seventy-two.
